I think they're talking more about letting kids be challenged. Instead of protecting your kids from anything scary or stressful, you work through these things with them, which teaches them how to handle scary and stressful situations in a healthy manner. In the end they'll be more comfortable and competent adults because they aren't worried by pressure or by challenges.

Even in extreme stress, some people blossom beautifully. Elie Wiesel would not be the man he is without having survived Auschwitz and Buchenwald. However that doesn't mean it's good to send your kid to a concentration camp because they might eventually win the Nobel Peace Prize.

However the opposite - complete lack of stress creates adults who lack the resilience to deal with even the most minor things. (Of which I am painfully aware as an ER doctor in a college town with a lot of sheltered snowflakes).

But it's really 2 bell curves on different axes - one being how much stress the child endures and one being the innate resilience that the child brings to those experiences as well as their development that has occurred before the stressful experience. Someone like Elie Wiesel would probably be OK in any circumstance in which he just survived. Most people not so much. But even with the most resilient of kids, there will be some damage that happens with enough stress.
